name: securelevel
description:
SECURELEVEL 1 MAKES A MOUNTED FILESYSTEM'S RAW DEVICE READ-ONLY, and the two halves are asserted on ONE boot because they are one claim.  apple/fgx#410.

THE EFFECT, second command.  `fsck -f' with no `-n' on the live root opens /dev/rsd0 for reading and then for WRITING; setup.c prints ` (NO WRITE)' when the second open fails (2.11BSD usr/sbin/fsck/setup.c, `if (nflag || (fswritefd = open(dev, O_WRONLY)) < 0)').  So the string is fsck reporting that the kernel refused it -- and refusing it is the point: before this the same command would have repaired a filesystem with daemons running on it.  READING STILL WORKS, which the five phases and rc=0 say; that asymmetry is upstream's design (the securelevel clause sits inside `if (mode & FWRITE)', sys_inode.c:650) and is how an operator finds out whether the machine needs to come down.

MEASURED DISCRIMINATING: on the build where init's raise silently failed -- the argument block was read from the wrong stack offset, so every sysctl answered EINVAL and getsecuritylevel returned -1 -- this exact command printed `** /dev/rsd0' with no `(NO WRITE)' and repaired away.  THE GATE ALONE IS NOT THE FEATURE: spec_open's check cannot fire while the level is 0, which is the dead-check shape apple/fgx#406 turned out to be, so the raise and the gate are tested together or nothing is tested.

THE SYSCALL, first command.  sysctltest asserts what the fsck line cannot see: that the level reads back as 1 on a multiuser machine, that an unserved name answers ENOTSUP at both the top level and the leaf, and -- the one that is a security rule rather than an interface detail -- that a process which is not pid 1 cannot LOWER the level, AND that the level is unchanged after the refusal.  A rule that returned EPERM having already written would be no rule, and nothing about a machine that quietly dropped to level 0 would look wrong.
